newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Tumbling Czech stocks face further slide -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Tumbling Czech stocks face further slide -analysts.

text.p: Leading Czech shares, which have fallen around 12 percent in the last six bourse sessions, face further sharp losses as the main Prague index dives on profit taking and currency nervousness, analysts say.

On Wednesday the PX50 index fell 13.8 points or 2.3 percent to 584.7, leaving it seven percent below last Wednesday's opening. One senior analyst, who requested anonymity, said it could drop below 550 before recovering.

The drop has been even more marked among the Prague Stock Exchange's (PSE) most heavily weighted shares -- SPT Telecom a.s., power utility CEZ a.s. and Komercni Banka a.s. -- which taken together account for 45 percent of the PX50's total capitalisation.
The three issues have fallen by an average of 12 percent in the last six sessions alone.
"I could imagine that it (the downtrend) will take a few days more," said Pavel Sobisek, chief equities analyst at Zivnostenska Banka.
Analysts and dealers told Reuters that the fall in Czech equities was not unique, although it had been much more pronounced than in central Europe's other main bourses.

"There are no foreign investors right now. But this is not peculiar to the Czech Republic. Poland and Hungary are also (affected). We're going through a bit of a pause right now," said Alex Angell of Wood and Company.

The Polish WIG index has fallen 582 points, 3.2 percent, in the last week, closing on Wednesday at 17,539.9 while the Budapest BUX was down 143.64 points, 2.6 percent, to 5,451.88 over the same period.

Analysts also pointed to two special factors which have caused the Czech market to fall so sharply: the speed of the PX50's ascent in the first two months of the year and foreign investor concerns about the fate of the Czech crown.

The PX50 surged at the beginning of the year, rising 16.5 percent to a peak of 629 in the middle of February. Many players said the rise was not driven by fundamentals and that the volatility was typical of emerging markets.
"You can't expect these markets to go up so much without profit taking," said John Vax of ING Barings.
"I'm not surprised (by the fall) because I did not believe that gains in the first months were justified," added Sobisek.
Foreign confidence in the Czech market has also been dented by risk on the crown which has fallen sharply in the last few sessions.

"I think one of the main reasons (for the decline) is because crown depreciation is possible...Major isssues (are especially vulnerable) because of interest from foreign investors," said Petr Opocensky of Citicorp Securities.

Foreign investors normally account for at least half of daily turnover in the major issues and a buying spree at the beginning of the year by such investors provoked a sustained bull run which lasted for most of January and February.
During that period, the Czech crown appreciated strongly against the dollar and mark but in recent sessions it has fallen back to levels not seen since before Christmas.

On Wednesday, the central bank fixed the crown, which is tied to a basket consisting 65 percent of marks and 35 percent of dollars, at 29.378 versus the dollar and 17.162 against the mark, 1.86 percent above the basket mid-point and compared with a high of 5.51 percent in early February.
